cls: Reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor + nicotinic receptor modulator
quick: IR 4 mg BID; ER 8 mg daily; titrate to 16-24 mg/day
Take with food (morning and evening meals)
Limited data; use only if clearly needed
Not recommended; unknown excretion in milk
Moderate: max 16 mg/day; severe: not recommended
Avoid; CNS effects and ulcer/GI risk
Heart rate, weight, GI symptoms, cognition, syncope
summary: Galantamine is a reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that also allosterically potentiates nicotinic receptors, used to treat mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's dementia. It is started low and titrated (IR 4 mg twice daily or ER 8 mg once daily) to a target of 16-24 mg/day. Common effects are nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and weight loss; clinically important cautions include bradycardia/syncope, and it should not be used in severe renal (CrCl <9) or severe hepatic impairment.
indications: Treatment of mild to moderate dementia of the Alzheimer's type

dosage.n: Take with morning and evening meals

dosage.d: Increase to 8 mg BID for >=4 weeks, then 12 mg BID if needed (16-24 mg/day)
dosage.n: Increase at intervals of at least 4 weeks

dosage.d: Start 8 mg once daily; titrate to 16 mg, then 24 mg/day
dosage.n: Increase every 4 weeks; take with food

admin: Take with food (preferably morning and evening meals) to reduce GI side effects
Ensure adequate fluid intake during treatment
Swallow extended-release capsules whole; do not crush or chew
Titrate slowly with at least 4-week intervals between dose increases
If therapy is interrupted for several days or more, restart at the lowest dose and re-titrate
moa: Galantamine reversibly and competitively inhibits acetylcholinesterase, increasing acetylcholine availability at central cholinergic synapses. It also acts as an allosteric potentiating ligand at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, enhancing cholinergic neurotransmission thought to underlie symptomatic cognitive benefit in Alzheimer's disease.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to galantamine or formulation components
relative: Sick sinus syndrome or other supraventricular conduction abnormalities
History of peptic ulcer disease or GI bleeding / NSAID use
Asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
monitor: GI bleeding signs in at-risk patients

preg: There are limited data in pregnant women. Use only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus; cholinergic effects could theoretically affect the fetus/neonate.
lact: It is not known whether galantamine is excreted in human milk. Because of potential cholinergic effects in the infant, breastfeeding is not recommended during therapy.
renal: No dose adjustment for mild-to-moderate renal impairment up to CrCl ~9-60, but do not exceed 16 mg/day in moderate impairment. In severe renal impairment (CrCl <9 mL/min), galantamine is not recommended.
hepatic: Use is not recommended in severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh 10-15). In moderate impairment (Child-Pugh 7-9), titrate slowly and do not exceed 16 mg/day. No adjustment for mild impairment.

major: Beta-blockers / other bradycardic agents (digoxin, diltiazem) - additive bradycardia, heart block
Succinylcholine and similar neuromuscular blockers - prolonged/exaggerated neuromuscular blockade
Anticholinergic drugs - antagonize galantamine and worsen cognition
moderate: Strong CYP2D6 inhibitors (paroxetine, quinidine) - increased galantamine levels
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, erythromycin) - increased galantamine levels
minor: Cimetidine - modest increase in galantamine bioavailability
interactions.food: Take with food to slow absorption and reduce nausea; food does not reduce overall absorption.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol; it adds CNS effects and increases GI irritation/ulcer risk.
interactions.diagnostics: No characteristic lab interference; monitor for weight loss and bradycardia clinically.

serious: Serious skin reactions (SJS, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis)

monitoring: Heart rate and rhythm; watch for syncope and falls
GI symptoms and signs of bleeding in at-risk patients
Hydration and renal function during GI illness
counsel: Take with breakfast and evening meal (or with breakfast for once-daily ER) to lessen stomach upset
Drink plenty of fluids, especially if you have vomiting or diarrhea
Report fainting, slow heartbeat, black/tarry stools or severe stomach pain
Do not crush or chew the extended-release capsules
If you stop the medicine for a few days, do not restart at the old dose - contact your doctor to re-titrate
This treats symptoms; it does not cure Alzheimer's disease
pk: Symptomatic benefit develops over weeks of therapy
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect from moisture
pearls: Causes bradycardia and syncope - use caution with beta-blockers and in cardiac conduction disease
Avoid in severe renal (CrCl <9) and severe hepatic impairment; cap at 16 mg/day in moderate impairment
Always re-titrate from the lowest dose if treatment has been interrupted for several days
Dual mechanism: cholinesterase inhibition plus nicotinic receptor allosteric potentiation
May prolong/intensify succinylcholine-type neuromuscular blockade during anesthesia
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember unless it is near the next dose, in which case skip it. Never take two doses at once. If several days are missed, contact the prescriber to restart at the lowest dose and re-titrate.
overdose: Overdose can cause a cholinergic crisis: severe nausea, vomiting, salivation, sweating, bradycardia, hypotension, muscle weakness/fasciculation, convulsions and respiratory depression. Treatment is supportive; intravenous atropine is the antidote for severe cholinergic effects. Maintain airway and supportive care.
